analogy.p: Standing near a campfire is like irradiation: you feel the heat while you are close, and the moment you walk away (or put up a screen) it stops, and you are not hot yourself. Getting glowing embers stuck on your clothes is like contamination: the embers go with you and keep heating you wherever you go until you brush them off or they burn out. The shorter the time an ember glows, the sooner the danger ends, like a short half-life. Where it breaks down: heat is not ionising radiation, and embers burn out in a predictable way, whereas the exact moment each nucleus decays is random.

bullets: **Irradiation** = exposure of an object (or person) to nuclear radiation from a source **outside** the object.
**Contamination** = the **unwanted presence of materials containing radioactive atoms** on other materials (including on or inside a person).
You must know the **hazards of each** and be able to **compare** them.
You must explain how the hazard depends on the **type of radiation** (alpha, beta, gamma) and on the **half-life**.
You must know sensible **precautions** and **correct handling** of sources.
You should be able to explain why research on the effects of radiation is **published and peer reviewed** (see later section).
This is a Paper 1 topic (4.4 Atomic structure) and links to half-life and uses of radiation.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: For this point you must be aware of the **dangers of ionising radiation** in terms of **irradiation** and **contamination**, and be able to say what the hazards of each are. You must also understand why the hazards associated with radioactive material **differ according to the type of radiation emitted and its half-life**, and know that **suitable precautions must be taken** to protect against any hazard a radioactive source might involve, including **correct handling of radioactive materials**. Examiners love comparison questions, so the real skill is being able to contrast the two ideas clearly using the exact words below.

bullets: **Ionisation** is the removal of electrons from atoms, producing positive ions.
Damage to **DNA** can cause **mutations**, which may lead to **cancer** many years later.
High doses can **kill cells** directly, causing radiation sickness, hair loss and burns.
Low doses spread over time are usually repaired, but the risk of harm is never exactly zero.
The harm happens because energy is **absorbed by the tissue**, so radiation absorbed in the body matters most.
The effects are not immediate for low doses, which is why the danger is easy to underestimate.
Alpha is the **most ionising**, gamma the **least ionising**, with beta in between.
Penetration is the opposite: gamma penetrates most, alpha least.
core.h: Ionising radiation and why it is hazardous
core.p: Alpha particles, beta particles and gamma rays are all **ionising radiation**: they have enough energy to knock electrons off atoms, turning them into ions. When this happens inside living cells it can damage **DNA** and other important molecules. If the damage is not repaired correctly the cell may mutate and divide uncontrollably, which is **cancer**, or the cell may simply die. Large doses kill so many cells that tissues stop working, which causes **radiation sickness** and burns. The hazard of a radioactive source is therefore all about how much ionisation it causes in living tissue.

bullets: Source is **outside** the object being exposed.
The irradiated object does **not** become radioactive (it has no radioactive atoms added).
Irradiation **stops** as soon as the source is removed, shielded or the object moves away.
The hazard depends on the **dose received**, which depends on the type of radiation, its energy, the time exposed and the distance.
Gamma rays are the biggest irradiation hazard because they **penetrate** the body easily.
Alpha irradiation from outside is **low risk** because alpha is absorbed by a few centimetres of air and by the dead outer layer of skin.
Beta irradiation can penetrate skin and cause burns or damage to tissue just below the surface.
Useful irradiation includes **sterilising** medical equipment and food, and **radiotherapy** to destroy tumours.
core.p: **Irradiation** happens when an object is exposed to nuclear radiation from a source that is **outside** it. The radiation travels from the source, through air, and into the object. The vital idea is that an irradiated object **does not become radioactive** itself. When the source is switched off, removed or shielded, the irradiation stops immediately. An X-ray of a broken arm, standing too close to a gamma source in a laboratory, and food being sterilised with gamma rays are all examples of irradiation.

bullets: The contaminating atoms are **on or in** the object, so the object itself becomes a source of radiation.
The hazard is due to the **decay of the contaminating atoms**.
Contamination continues as long as the atoms are present, so it can last for a long time.
Contamination can be **spread** from place to place on hands, tools, clothes and dust.
Routes into the body: **breathing in** radioactive dust or gas, **swallowing** (eating or drinking with contaminated hands), and **entering through cuts** in the skin.
Once inside, the body cannot easily get away from the radiation, so every decay irradiates cells **from the inside**.
Treatment includes removing contaminated clothing, washing the skin and, for internal contamination, medical treatment to help remove the material.
Example: after a nuclear accident, radioactive dust can settle on crops, land and buildings.
core.h: Contamination: radioactive atoms where they should not be
core.p: **Contamination** is the **unwanted presence of materials containing radioactive atoms** on other materials. If a person is contaminated, radioactive atoms are on their skin, clothes or hair, or have got **inside** their body. The hazard from a contaminated object is due to the **decay of the contaminating atoms**. Unlike irradiation, you cannot simply step away from the source, because the source is stuck to you or inside you and is continuing to decay and release radiation until the atoms are removed or have decayed away.

bullets: **Where is the source?** Irradiation: outside the object. Contamination: on or inside the object.
**Does the object become radioactive?** Irradiation: no. Contamination: yes, it now carries radioactive atoms.
**Duration:** irradiation ends when the source is removed or shielded; contamination continues until the atoms are removed or decay.
**Protection:** irradiation is reduced by shielding, distance and time; contamination is prevented by keeping the source sealed and not letting it touch or enter you (gloves, tongs, no eating).
**Worst type of radiation:** outside the body, gamma is the greatest danger; inside the body, alpha is the greatest danger.
**Common link:** both can cause harm because radiation ionises cells and damages DNA.
Contamination can lead to **irradiation** of the person, because the contaminating atoms irradiate the body.
Irradiation can never cause contamination by itself, because no radioactive material is transferred.
core.h: Irradiation versus contamination: the key comparison
core.p: Most exam marks on this topic come from a clear comparison. The cleanest way is to compare **where the source is**, whether the object **becomes radioactive**, **how long** the exposure lasts and **how you protect yourself**. Always write complete comparative sentences such as 'irradiation stops when the source is removed, whereas contamination continues until the radioactive atoms are removed or decay'.

bullets: **Alpha** (helium nucleus): range of a few centimetres in air, stopped by paper or dead skin; very strongly ionising. **Outside = low hazard; inside = very high hazard** because all its energy is absorbed in a very small volume of tissue.
**Beta** (fast electron): stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium; moderately ionising and moderately penetrating. Hazard is **moderate both outside and inside**.

**Gamma** (electromagnetic wave): very penetrating, reduced but never completely stopped by thick lead or concrete; weakly ionising. **Outside = high hazard; inside = lower hazard** as much of the radiation passes straight out of the body.
Because alpha is so dangerous when inside, **alpha sources must never be swallowed or inhaled**, e.g. radon gas is dangerous when breathed in for this reason.
Because gamma is dangerous from a distance, thick shielding and distance are needed for gamma sources.
Neutron radiation is also hazardous and is penetrating; it can make materials radioactive.
In exam answers always link the **property** (ionising or penetrating) to the **location** (inside or outside the body).
Do not say gamma is 'harmless inside': it is lower risk, not no risk.
core.h: Why the hazard depends on the type of radiation
core.p: Alpha, beta and gamma radiation differ in **ionising power** and **penetrating power**, and these two properties swap in importance depending on whether the source is outside or inside the body. Outside the body, what matters is whether the radiation can get through the skin to reach living cells, so **penetration** is key and gamma is worst. Inside the body there is nothing to stop the radiation reaching tissue, so what matters is how much damage it does when absorbed, so **ionising power** is key and alpha is worst.

bullets: Short half-life: **high initial activity**, so intense radiation, but it **decays away quickly**.
Long half-life: **lower activity** at any moment, but it **remains hazardous for a long time**.
For the same number of atoms, the shorter the half-life, the higher the activity, because more nuclei decay each second.
Medical tracers are chosen to have a **short half-life** (hours) so the patient is only radioactive briefly.
Nuclear waste containing long half-life isotopes must be stored safely for **thousands of years or more**.
A source with a very long half-life gives almost constant radiation, making it a long-term contamination problem.
Contamination by a long half-life, alpha-emitting isotope is among the worst combinations: it stays for a long time and does most damage inside the body.
Use both ideas in an answer: **type of radiation** AND **half-life**.
core.h: Why the hazard depends on half-life
core.p: **Half-life** is the time taken for the number of radioactive nuclei in a sample to halve, or for the count rate (or activity) to fall to half its initial value. The half-life affects the hazard in two opposite ways. A **short half-life** means the atoms decay very quickly, so the **activity is very high at the start** (lots of radiation per second) but the source soon becomes safe. A **long half-life** means the activity is lower but the material stays radioactive for a very long time, so a contaminated area or body may remain dangerous for years.

bullets: **Inhalation**: breathing in radioactive dust or gas such as radon.
**Ingestion**: swallowing atoms from contaminated food, drink or hands.
**Absorption through skin** or entry through **cuts and wounds**.
**Spread by touch**: from gloves or tools to door handles, benches and other people.
Sealed sources are designed so that radioactive atoms cannot leak out, even though the radiation can escape.
Unsealed sources, such as liquid tracers, are the main contamination risk.
Radioactive dust after an accident can contaminate soil, water and food chains, so people far away can be contaminated.
Decontamination removes the atoms, whereas shielding only blocks radiation.
core.h: How contamination spreads and gets into the body
core.p: The danger of contamination is that radioactive atoms are **small and easily moved**. They can be carried on dust, in liquids, on gloves and tools, or as a gas. Once the atoms have moved from the source to a person or surface, that person or surface is a source in its own right. This is why laboratory and hospital rules are so strict about keeping radioactive sources in sealed containers and not touching them with bare hands.

bullets: **Time**: spend as little time near the source as possible.
**Distance**: stay as far away as practical and use **tongs** or remote handling.
**Shielding**: lead aprons, lead-lined walls, concrete barriers and lead-glass screens.
Operators of X-ray machines **stand behind a screen** or leave the room.
Sources are **stored in lead-lined containers**, in locked cupboards, and returned straight after use.
**Film badges** or dosimeters are worn by workers so their exposure can be monitored.
A source should be **pointed away** from people and never aimed at anyone.
Different radiation needs different shielding: paper for alpha, aluminium for beta, lead for gamma.
core.p: Because irradiation depends on the dose of radiation reaching the body, the main protections are to **reduce the time** of exposure, **increase the distance** from the source and place **shielding** between the source and the person. The radiation from a point source spreads out, and the air also absorbs some of it, so the further away you are the smaller the dose. Gamma needs dense materials such as **lead** or thick **concrete**.

bullets: Use **tongs** or forceps, never bare hands, to move sources.
Wear **gloves, lab coats and sometimes masks** so atoms do not reach skin or get breathed in.
**No eating, drinking or touching your face** in areas where radioactive materials are used.
**Wash hands** and monitor for contamination after work.
Use **sealed containers** and work over trays to catch spills.
Dispose of radioactive waste in **designated, clearly labelled containers**.
After an accident, remove outer clothing, wash and monitor people to check for contamination.
Because contamination persists, clean-up and monitoring must continue until the radiation level is safe.
core.p: Preventing contamination means making sure radioactive atoms **never leave the source** and never reach skin, clothing, food or the air you breathe. This is done by keeping materials sealed, handling them with tools rather than hands, and following strict hygiene. Protective clothing makes it possible to remove contaminated items before the atoms spread further.

bullets: Handle with **tongs** to keep the source away from skin (increases distance, avoids contamination).
Hold the source **pointing away** from yourself and others.
Keep exposure **short** and return the source to a **lead-lined box** straight away.
Keep the source **at arm's length / as far from people as possible**.
For alpha, remember the source is only really dangerous if **swallowed or inhaled**, so avoid any contact and wash hands.
For gamma, shielding and distance are the key precautions.
Always give a **reason**: 'to reduce the time of exposure', 'to prevent contamination', 'to absorb the radiation'.
Teachers store sources locked away and keep a **record** of their use.
core.h: Handling radioactive sources: the exam and school context
core.p: The specification states that suitable precautions must be taken to protect against any hazard that the radioactive source used in an exam might involve. This means that, whichever source an exam question describes, you should name the radiation it emits and suggest precautions matching it. A common mark-scheme approach is to give one mark for the precaution and one mark for the reason.

bullets: **Publishing** shares results so other scientists can build on them and check them.
**Peer review** = independent experts in the same field scrutinise the work before publication.
It reduces **bias**, errors and unjustified claims.
Reliable evidence is needed because **long-term effects** such as cancer take years to appear.
Safe working limits and safety rules are based on this evidence.
Workers wear **film badges** or electronic dosimeters to check their dose.
The public may perceive radiation risks as bigger than they are because the effects are invisible and the word 'nuclear' sounds frightening.
Always weigh **risk against benefit**, for example medical scans carry a small risk but give important information.
core.h: Monitoring exposure and the role of published research
core.p: Scientists have learned about the effects of radiation on the human body by studying patients, workers and survivors of nuclear accidents. It is important that the results of such studies are **published** so other scientists can see them, and **peer reviewed**, which means other independent experts check the methods and conclusions before they are accepted. This makes the findings more **reliable and valid**, helps to set safe limits for workers and the public, and means the evidence can be **replicated** by other researchers.

bullets: Half-life link: after each half-life the activity halves, so a contaminant with a 6 hour half-life is 1/16 of its original activity after 24 hours.
Type link: an alpha emitter in the lungs (from radon) is a contamination hazard.
Uses link: medical tracers are gamma emitters with short half-lives to limit harm to the patient.
Waste link: long half-life waste must be stored securely for a very long time.
Background radiation link: some radiation is always present, so dose from a source is compared with this normal level.
Evaluate by stating the **hazard**, the **precaution** and the **benefit**.
In extended answers use linking words: 'because', 'therefore', 'whereas'.
Always check whether the question refers to the source being **inside** or **outside** the body, as that decides which radiation is worst.
core.h: Link to other topics and Higher tier thinking
core.p: This topic links strongly to several others. **Half-life** (4.4.2) tells you how long a contaminating source stays dangerous. **Types of radiation** (4.4.2) tells you the penetration and ionising properties. **Uses of radiation** such as tracers and radiotherapy (4.4.3) rely on picking a source whose hazard is acceptable, for example a short half-life tracer. **Nuclear power** and waste link to long-term contamination. Higher-tier questions often ask you to evaluate a situation, choose the best isotope and justify it using type of radiation and half-life together.

exam: **Command words:** 'Compare' needs similarities/differences in both items using comparative language; 'Explain' needs a reason with 'because'; 'Describe' needs facts only.
**2 marks (define):** Irradiation = exposure of an object to radiation from a source outside the object; contamination = unwanted presence of radioactive atoms on or in an object.
**Comparison (3-4 marks):** give where the source is, whether the object becomes radioactive, and how long the exposure lasts or how to stop it.
**'Why is alpha dangerous inside the body?'** Model phrases: 'strongly ionising', 'all the energy is absorbed by cells', 'damages DNA / causes cancer'.
**'Why is gamma dangerous outside the body?'** Model phrases: 'very penetrating', 'passes through the skin to reach organs', 'only reduced by thick lead or concrete'.
**Precautions questions:** give the precaution AND the reason, e.g. 'use tongs to increase the distance from the source, reducing the dose'.
**Half-life links:** mention both initial activity and how long the source stays radioactive.
**6 mark answers:** structure into irradiation, contamination, then type and half-life, ending with a short conclusion.
**Data questions:** if a graph of activity is given, read half-lives by finding the time for the activity to halve.
**Evaluate/Suggest:** always balance the risk (hazard) against the benefit and say whether the precautions make the risk acceptable.
**Avoid** vague words such as 'dangerous' without saying why (ionisation, DNA damage, cancer).

mistakes.r: An irradiated object does NOT become radioactive; only contamination adds radioactive atoms.
Contamination is the unwanted presence of materials containing radioactive atoms on or in the object.
mistakes.w: Contamination is when radiation touches you.

mistakes.r: Alpha is low risk outside the body but the MOST dangerous inside the body because it is strongly ionising.
mistakes.w: Alpha is harmless because it is stopped by paper.

mistakes.r: Gamma is the greatest hazard from outside the body because it is very penetrating.
mistakes.w: Gamma is not dangerous because it is weakly ionising.

mistakes.r: A long half-life means it stays radioactive for a long time; a short half-life means high activity at first but it decays quickly. Say both sides.
mistakes.w: A long half-life means a source is safer.

mistakes.r: Lead shields against radiation (irradiation); preventing contamination needs sealed sources, gloves and hygiene.
mistakes.w: Wearing lead protects against all contamination.

mistakes.r: Shielding absorbs the radiation but does not change the rate of decay of the nuclei.
mistakes.w: The source decays faster if you shield it.

mistakes.r: Say tongs increase the distance and prevent contamination of the hands, so the dose is reduced.

summary: The specification asks you to define irradiation (exposure from a source outside the body) and contamination (unwanted radioactive atoms on or inside an object), compare their hazards, and explain how hazards depend on the type of radiation and half-life. You must also know the precautions and correct handling of sources. It matters because it explains how people stay safe around radioactive materials.

terms.d: Radiation with enough energy to remove electrons from atoms, forming ions; includes alpha, beta and gamma.
The exposure of an object to nuclear radiation from a source outside the object. The irradiated object does not become radioactive.
The unwanted presence of materials containing radioactive atoms on other materials. The hazard is due to the decay of the contaminating atoms.
The random process in which an unstable nucleus emits radiation to become more stable.
The time taken for the number of radioactive nuclei in an isotope to halve, or the time for the count rate (or activity) from a sample to fall to half its initial level.
The rate at which a source of unstable nuclei decays, measured in becquerel (Bq).
The number of decays per second (or minute) detected by a Geiger-Muller tube and counter.
Two neutrons and two protons (a helium nucleus); strongly ionising, weakly penetrating.
A high-speed electron emitted from the nucleus when a neutron changes to a proton; moderately ionising and penetrating.
Electromagnetic radiation from the nucleus; weakly ionising, very penetrating.
Dense material placed between a source and a person to absorb radiation, e.g. lead.
A source in a closed container so radioactive atoms cannot escape, though radiation can.
Checking of scientific work by independent experts before it is published.
A badge containing photographic film that darkens with radiation, used to monitor a worker's exposure.
A measure of the harm to living tissue caused by exposure to radiation, measured in sieverts (Sv).

worked.ans: Irradiation = exposure from an external source and the object does not become radioactive; contamination = unwanted radioactive atoms on or in the object, so the hazard lasts until they are removed or decay.
worked.q: Explain the difference between irradiation and contamination. (4 marks)
steps: Irradiation: the object is exposed to radiation from a source outside the object (1).
The irradiated object does not become radioactive, and exposure stops when the source is removed or shielded (1).
Contamination: radioactive atoms are on or inside the object (1).
The object is a source of radiation until the atoms are removed or decay, so exposure continues (1).

worked.ans: The statement is only partly correct: alpha is low risk outside the body but very hazardous if the source is inside the body, because it is strongly ionising.
worked.q: A student says 'alpha radiation is safe because it cannot pass through paper'. Evaluate this statement. (4 marks)
steps: Outside the body alpha is low risk because it travels only a few centimetres in air and is absorbed by dead skin (1).
If an alpha emitter is swallowed or breathed in, all its energy is absorbed by cells in a very small region (1).
This can damage DNA and cause cancer, so the statement is only true for irradiation from outside, not for contamination (1).

worked.ans: Activity after 24 hours = 15 MBq (1/16 of the original). A short half-life limits the time the patient is contaminated, reducing the dose and risk.
worked.q: A patient is given a gamma-emitting tracer with a half-life of 6 hours and an initial activity of 240 MBq. Calculate the activity after 24 hours and explain why a short half-life is chosen. (4 marks, Higher)
steps: A short half-life means the tracer decays quickly, so the patient is contaminated for only a short time.
Gamma passes out of the body to be detected, and it is weakly ionising, so less damage is done inside the body.
